doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: First hearing jazz on a clip-on radio as a child
summary: His father gave him a clip-on radio at about eight and he heard jazz, probably Mack the Knife, on San Francisco radio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Ah — to live vicariously what others were doing. Do you recall what music you heard as a child that might have had something to do with your path in life?

You know I sort of do and sort of don’t. I remember my father gave me one of those clip- on unpowered radios. I don’t know if you remember that. It just has an alligator clip, you put it on your lampshade next to your bed and it receives stations. So I must have been like eight years old or something, and I remember hearing jazz and being knocked out, and I don’t even know what it was. I have a feeling it was probably Bobby Darin’s “Mack the Knife” with the big band, because that was something that would have been played on San Francisco AM radio, gotten into mainstream enough that an elementary kid would hear it. But you know I always, from when I became conscious of music and developed my love for it, it was jazz and popular music. You know I could give you later dates than that of things that I specifically remember but I wasn’t one of these three year olds that looked at the cello and decided that I wanted to play it and that was it.
